Sanchay Wealth Technologies: Three Pillars and One Quarter

An Indian-context case on strategy, themes and the allocation of a quarter

1. Koregaon Park, Thursday night

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Thursday, 22 October 2026, Devika Rane sat on the floor of her flat in Koregaon Park, Pune, with two laptops open and a plate of cold thepla beside her, trying to work out which of three documents she believed. The first was the slide the board had approved in January, which said Sanchay Wealth Technologies would spend FY27 on three pillars: deepen the portfolio, win the NRI corridor, own the workplace. The second was a spreadsheet of sixty-one backlog items, each scored on Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort by whichever product manager proposed it, ranked from 34.2 down to 0.3. The third was a one-page note from Ritika Banerjee in Toronto, sent at 6:04 that evening, whose second paragraph said in the flattest possible language that the analysis underpinning the second pillar rested on a denominator nobody had checked.

The board strategy review was at ten the next morning in Lower Parel, and Aniruddh Kamat, co-founder and chief executive, had asked for one slide: how the next quarter's engineering capacity would be divided, by pillar, in person-weeks. It sounded like a formatting exercise. Between the pre-Diwali freeze, a contractual go-live in Dubai on 15 January, a compliance deadline nobody could negotiate, and an earn-out worth ₹14 crore that made a colleague care intensely about a number she thought meaningless, Devika had 232 usable person-weeks and four constituencies who each believed, with evidence, that their work was the strategy. She had been told to make prioritisation follow the strategy. At 11:15 p.m. she was no longer sure the company had one strategy, or three, or none.

2. The company

Sanchay Wealth Technologies Private Limited was founded in Pune in 2019 by Aniruddh Kamat, formerly of a Mumbai asset manager's digital team, and Rukmini Iyer, an engineer who had spent six years building order-management systems for brokerages. Their premise was ordinary and correct: Indian households were moving savings out of fixed deposits and gold into mutual funds, and almost nobody outside the metros had a tool showing what they owned in one place. The app let a user buy direct plans, start a SIP on UPI AutoPay, import holdings from the registrars and track it all against goals. By the close of FY26 the platform carried ₹31,400 crore of assets and 47 lakh registered users, 11.2 lakh of whom transacted, and earned ₹96 crore: ₹58 crore from subscriptions at ₹899 and ₹2,499 a year, ₹19 crore from employers offering Sanchay as a workplace benefit, ₹7 crore from the NRI corridor, and ₹12 crore from an API business selling onboarding infrastructure to smaller distributors.

One earlier decision shaped everything Devika could do in October. In November 2022, flush from a Series B, Sanchay acquired Potli Savings, a Jaipur company whose app reminded 19 lakh small-ticket savers to run their SIPs and recurring deposits. The price was ₹38 crore, of which ₹14 crore was an earn-out payable in March 2027 if combined monthly active users stayed above 26 lakh for three consecutive months. Rukmini had argued for a six-month migration folding Potli into the main app; the board, wanting the earn-out metric clean and the acquired users undisturbed, chose to run Potli separately. Four years on it still ran on its own codebase, still served 17.8 lakh monthly actives, and still consumed five engineers and two support staff who could not be redeployed without moving a number the company had contractually promised to protect.

3. The industry

By 2026 the Indian mutual-fund industry had crossed ₹80 lakh crore of assets, with monthly SIP inflows near ₹31,000 crore, and distribution had become the most crowded part of Indian fintech. Groww and Zerodha's Coin had the scale; Angel One, Paytm Money, INDmoney, Kuvera and ET Money each held a slice; HDFC Bank and ICICI Direct still moved the largest tickets; and the Jio BlackRock joint venture had turned every investor conversation to distribution economics rather than growth. SEBI's execution-only-platform framework had, since 2023, formalised what companies like Sanchay were allowed to be: a registered platform executing direct-plan transactions without advice, under AMFI supervision, with a firm line between execution and recommendation. AMFI's MF Central had meanwhile commoditised the holdings-import feature that was once Sanchay's differentiator.

Three regulatory forces bore on the quarter. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent obligations required re-architecting how Sanchay collected, stored and withdrew consent, including for Potli users who had signed up under a different entity in 2021 and had never been re-consented. SEBI's attention to gamified engagement had produced an August consultation paper proposing restrictions on streaks, leaderboards and reward-linked nudges, with a standardised cost disclosure at the point of transaction. And the newest revenue line depended on IFSCA's GIFT City regime, under which non-resident Indians could invest through a feeder structure. Sanchay's global exposure ran entirely through that corridor: a June 2026 agreement with Durrah Remit FZE, a Dubai exchange house with 41 branches across the UAE and Oman, whose two lakh remitting customers were exactly the salaried Malayali, Telugu and Punjabi diaspora Sanchay wanted. The contract carried a first-year minimum guarantee of ₹6.75 crore, a 45 percent revenue share to Durrah, a co-branded white-label app, a go-live of 15 January 2027, a penalty of 20 percent of the year-one fee, and 24-month exclusivity barring any other Gulf exchange house.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The three pillars were written in a room in January. Aniruddh had returned from Singapore convinced that Sanchay's next round would be priced on international revenue and assets per user rather than registered users, and a two-day offsite converted that conviction into Exhibit 1. Nobody objected. Devika remembered the meeting as unusually harmonious, which she now regarded as a warning sign.

The evidence for the second pillar came from an analysis Ritika Banerjee ran in December. Users whose registered address was in the Gulf held 3.4 times the assets of the average Indian retail user. The number travelled: into the January deck, a March term-sheet conversation, the May Durrah negotiation, the pricing Aniruddh accepted in June. Ritika's October note said the comparison had two defects. The Gulf denominator counted only users who had completed a first transaction, while the retail comparison counted every user who had completed KYC — a difference of roughly 2.9 times in activation. And the numerator included 41 accounts of high-net-worth Indian users who had updated their address after relocating, each transferring an existing portfolio in one lump. Stripped of both effects, her revised estimate of the corridor's asset advantage was 1.1 to 1.6 times, an interval she declined to narrow because the cleaned sample was 380 users.

Meanwhile the first pillar had quietly stalled. The consolidated-portfolio work — importing holdings from other platforms, reconciling them, showing one net-worth view — shipped in April to poor reception. Tobias Kerner's research in Berlin found that users did not trust imported numbers they could not audit, and that the feature's commonest use was a single look followed by abandonment. An audit trail shipped in July and moved nothing. The third pillar, workplace, had gone better than expected: 46 employers, ₹19 crore of FY26 revenue growing at 71 percent, and an anchor client, Jhelum Auto Components, 18,000 employees across Pune, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Pantnagar, whose ₹2.4 crore contract came up for renewal on 31 December.

Then September happened. Jhelum's payroll-linked SIP deductions failed for 2,900 employees because of a UPI AutoPay mandate-limit change Sanchay's integration had not handled; the failures were fixed in nine days, but Jhelum's HR head wrote a letter using the phrase "material breach of service expectations." Durrah, the same week, added two requirements to the white-label build: UAE data residency for onboarding documents, and Arabic support hours Priya Menon's four-person Singapore team could not cover. And on 6 October, Nikhil Sequeira circulated a memo putting the DPDP consent re-architecture and the EOP disclosures in production before 31 March 2027 — which, given the Potli users needing re-consent, meant starting by November.

Figure A. Contractual dates were set in June against capacity assumed in January and an analysis re-examined only in October.

5. The people

Devika Rane, 36, VP Product, Pune, joined in 2021 from a payments company. Her position: the company cannot fund three pillars plus compliance plus Potli in one quarter, and someone must choose. Her incentive is a promotion to chief product officer that Aniruddh has hinted at twice and never scheduled. What she is not saying is that she does not believe workplace is a pillar at all — she thinks it is a business that happens to be working, which is different — and that she has never told Aniruddh she disagrees with the January framing, because she helped write it.

Aniruddh Kamat, 44, co-founder and CEO, splits his week between Pune and Mumbai. He wants the corridor funded to completion: Durrah is the centrepiece of the Series C narrative and the only part that is not a domestic market-share fight. His incentive is a round he expects to open in February. What he is not saying is that a lead investor's diligence checklist asks for international revenue above 15 percent, that the figure today is 7.3 percent, and that he has not read Ritika's note past the first paragraph.

Rukmini Iyer, 41, co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru, wants one quarter to retire the Potli stack: every quarter of delay costs five engineers and widens the compliance surface. Her incentive is an engineering organisation that can still hire. What she is not saying is that two senior engineers resigned in October, that she has not told Aniruddh, and that she was the one who agreed in 2022 to keep Potli separate.

Harsh Vora, 38, VP Growth, Jaipur, founder of Potli, wants the festival engagement programme — Dhanteras gold goals, streaks, referrals — funded before the Diwali freeze, and cites Exhibit 6 as proof that engagement drives everything else. His incentive is public: ₹14 crore of earn-out contingent on combined actives above 26 lakh. What he is not saying is that roughly a third of Potli's actives come from a notification loop the SEBI consultation would likely curb, and that a larger platform has approached him.

Priya Menon, 33, Head of Customer Success, Singapore, owns Durrah. She wants data residency and the white-label build funded now: a missed go-live triggers the ₹1.35 crore penalty and resets a relationship built over eight months. Her variable pay is tied to corridor assets. What she is not saying is that Durrah's own KYC operations team is four weeks behind on its side, which may make any slip mutual and the penalty unenforceable — something she has not put in writing to anyone in Pune.

Nikhil Sequeira, 49, Head of Compliance, Mumbai, is the designated principal officer and wants the DPDP and EOP work started in November, non-negotiably. His incentive is personal exposure. What he is not saying is that his fourteen-week estimate carries four weeks of padding added after an earlier overrun, and that a narrower scope covering only new consents could be done in nine.

Tobias Kerner, 35, Lead Product Designer, Berlin, wants the consolidated-portfolio experience rebuilt rather than patched: trust in the portfolio view, he argues, is the precondition for every other pillar, since an NRI will not move a lakh into an app whose numbers they cannot audit. His incentive is professional — eighteen months on a feature now called a failure internally. What he is not saying is that his research base is fourteen interviews, eleven with top-decile users.

Rajat Malhotra, 47, Head of Enterprise Sales, Edison, New Jersey, sells workplace to Indian subsidiaries of US employers and to GCC groups. He wants the Jhelum incident closed with visible engineering investment and three payroll integrations built. His quota is weighted 60 percent on new logos. What he is not saying is that two of his three pipeline logos will not decide before April, and that Jhelum has asked for a 12 percent reduction at renewal.

Ritika Banerjee, 31, Analytics Lead, Toronto, wants the corridor's assumptions re-tested before more capacity goes in. Her incentive is accuracy, and she is the only person here whose incentive points nowhere else. What she is not saying — or said only in a February document comment nobody opened — is that she flagged the activation mismatch eight months ago and let it go when no one replied.

Figure B. Six time zones, one backlog. The only window in which Pune, Berlin, Toronto and New Jersey can all meet is 45 minutes at 6:30 p.m. IST — the weekly prioritisation call.

7. Voices

"We agreed three pillars in January. I am not reopening the strategy six weeks before a round. I am asking for one slide that shows the board we are spending where we said we would spend."Aniruddh Kamat, to Devika Rane, call of 19 October

"Data residency is not a feature request, it is the condition their compliance head signed on. If it is not in the January build we do not go live, and then we are in penalty and I am the one who has to say so."Priya Menon, #corridor channel, 9 October, 7:12 p.m. IST

"We can discuss the definition of active all day. The agreement says combined MAU above 26 lakh. In September we were at 26.7. If the Dhanteras campaign does not run, we are at 25-point-something in November and December, and then we discuss definitions with lawyers."Harsh Vora, weekly call, 20 October

"Two of my people left last week. Start another quarter where the plan says portfolio and the calendar says firefighting and I lose two more — then none of these options exist."Rukmini Iyer, one-to-one with Devika Rane, 21 October

"I cannot sell integrations I have not been given engineers for. Tell me which quarter and I will sell that quarter."Rajat Malhotra, email, 20 October, 9:02 a.m. EDT

"We call the portfolio view a feature that failed. It did not fail, it was never finished. Nobody moves five lakh rupees into a screen that cannot show where its number came from — not in Pune, certainly not from Dubai."Tobias Kerner, design review, 15 October

8. The options, as Devika currently frames them

By Thursday night she had four options on a page, in the order she had thought of them, and suspected the order revealed more about her than about the company.

Option A: fund the three pillars in proportion to FY26 revenue. Portfolio and retail take the largest share, workplace next, the corridor a defensible slice. It is easy to explain and impossible to call favouritism. It also funds the past, and gives the corridor about 40 person-weeks against a contractual build Bengaluru estimated at 73 before data residency.

Option B: concentrate the quarter on the corridor and finish it properly. The Durrah build, data residency and feeder onboarding consume about 89 person-weeks; compliance takes its 60 to 90; everything else waits. This honours the contract and protects the Series C story, at the price of slipping the portfolio rebuild to April and probably missing the earn-out threshold — and it concentrates the quarter on the one pillar whose supporting evidence collapsed six hours ago.

Option C: let contracts and regulation decide, and stop calling it strategy. Fund the DPDP work, the EOP disclosures, the Durrah minimum for a technical go-live, the UPI mandate fix and the Jhelum remediation, and defend the rest as unaffordable. Exhibit 5 shows this is what the last two quarters did; it takes about 190 of the 232 person-weeks. The cost is a third quarter making nothing anyone chose.

Option D: re-cut the pillars around outcomes rather than segments — around trust in a consolidated portfolio, which Tobias argues underlies corridor and workplace alike, and around a retention number that does not depend on a definition of "active" written in 2022. Devika finds this the most satisfying and least presentable option, since it means telling a board that the slide it approved in January grouped work by who sells it rather than by what it should achieve.

What none of the four questions is the 232 person-weeks; Exhibit 5 suggests that number has never survived contact with a quarter, and real capacity may be nearer 140. Nor does any ask whether Potli's five engineers are genuinely unavailable or merely expensive to free. And all four take the pillars' metrics as given, when Exhibit 1's footnote records that they were written three months after approval by the people to be measured on them.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The review is at 10 a.m. on Friday, 23 October, in Lower Parel. Capacity for Q3 FY27 is 34 engineers over 11 usable weeks after the pre-Diwali freeze of 4 to 12 November: 374 gross person-weeks, of which the approved plan assumes 38 percent keeps the lights on, leaving 232. Hiring is frozen at 34 heads under a board cap on monthly burn of ₹6.75 crore; at ₹1.45 lakh per engineer-week, ten person-weeks reallocated is about ₹14.5 lakh. Cash is ₹138 crore, or 21 months at a burn of ₹6.4 crore, and Aniruddh intends to open the Series C in February on nine-month numbers. Durrah's go-live is 15 January 2027, with a ₹1.35 crore penalty and 24-month GCC exclusivity, so a failed corridor cannot be replaced with another partner. The ₹14 crore earn-out needs combined actives above 26 lakh for three consecutive months before March 2027; Exhibit 6 shows October at 25.7. The DPDP and EOP work must be in production before 31 March 2027, and Nikhil's fourteen-week estimate does not fit a quarter starting in January. Jhelum renews on 31 December at ₹2.4 crore, with a 12 percent reduction requested and a letter in the file using the words "material breach."

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 ranks a Dhanteras streak campaign at 34.2 and a contractual white-label build at 1.2. What is that ranking measuring, and what would you have to believe about Sanchay for the order to be right?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 describe the same four segments and reach opposite conclusions about the corridor. Which would you put before the board, and what must be added to either before it can inform a capacity decision?
  3. Each pillar in Exhibit 1 names a segment. Rewrite them as statements of the outcome each is meant to produce. Does the number of pillars change? Does the ranking in Exhibit 2?
  4. Harsh Vora's earn-out is known to everyone and tied to a metric defined four years ago. How should a product leader treat a colleague whose incentive is legitimate, contractual and pointed at the wrong number?
  5. Ritika's note arrives six hours before a board meeting and undermines a commitment already signed with a penalty clause. What obligation does Devika have to put it in the room, and what follows from each way she could handle it: raise it fully, summarise it, or wait?
  6. It is Monday morning, 26 October. Devika has one quarter, 232 nominal person-weeks that Exhibit 5 suggests are closer to 140, and eight colleagues who each hold part of the evidence. What does she do first, what does she stop, and what does she say to a board that approved three pillars in January and expects to see them funded?

11. Thursday night, continued

At twenty to one, Devika drafted a message to Aniruddh beginning "Before tomorrow, there is something in Ritika's note you should see," and did not send it. She opened the capacity slide again: four rows, three pillars and a line for compliance, the rightmost column adding to 232 whichever way she arranged them, every arrangement a sentence about what Sanchay was for. She thought about Priya, awake in Singapore; about the five engineers in Jaipur maintaining an app that earned ₹3.9 crore, cost ₹5.2 crore and held ₹14 crore hostage; about Tobias's fourteen interviews and the possibility that he was right anyway. Outside, a building was already strung with lights for Diwali. She saved the file without changing it and set an alarm for five.

Belan Analytics: Whose Backlog Item Goes First?

A teaching case on strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation

1. The Monday morning message

At 8:40 on the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Ananya Kulkarni was reading a WhatsApp message for the third time, on the terrace of Belan Analytics' office in Domlur, Bengaluru, a cutting chai going cold beside her laptop. The message was from Robert Fein, the company's global head of sales, writing from New Jersey the previous night. "Ananya, I need the Gulf localisation pack at the top of the Q3 build. Wahat signed on the promise of Arabic invoicing by January. If we slip this, we lose the story we're telling every other Gulf retailer." Ananya had six days before she had to walk into a conference room in Mumbai and hand the leadership team a finished roadmap for October through December, organised, as the CEO had insisted at the last board meeting, around three strategic pillars for the year. The backlog in front of her had forty-one open items, each scored by a different product manager using the company's RICE template, and the ranked list did not, on its own, tell her which items to fund with the thirty-odd engineering-weeks she actually had. Somewhere in that list was the right answer. Her job for the next six days was to find it before Robert, or the loudest voice that week, found it for her.

2. Belan Analytics

Belan Analytics Private Limited was founded in 2018 by two IIT Bombay classmates who had spent their first jobs building inventory systems for a Mumbai apparel chain and grown tired of watching stores discount stock that never needed discounting and run out of stock that always sold. Their product, ShelfSense, combined point-of-sale data, footfall counts, and local weather and festival calendars into a demand-sensing and pricing engine that told a category manager, store by store, what to price a product at and how much to order. By September 2026 the company had forty-six paying customers, ranging from a regional pharmacy chain in Kerala to two quick-commerce dark-store operators competing in the same cities as Zepto and Blinkit, and had grown annual recurring revenue to roughly ₹42 crore. It had no direct Indian competitor of its own size, but was constantly measured, in investor conversations, against the in-house data-science teams at Reliance Retail and DMart, and against the export story of Indian product companies such as Freshworks and Zoho — the bar every board member cited as what Belan needed to clear for a real Series C. Three months earlier, Belan had closed its first customer outside India: Wahat Retail Group, a hypermarket chain headquartered in Dubai, on an annual contract value of ₹6.1 crore, the largest deal in the company's history, and the one sales was already using to court three more Gulf prospects worth ₹9 crore in pipeline.

3. The situation

At the July board meeting, Belan's co-founder and CEO, Arjun Mehta, told the leadership team that FY27 needed three strategic pillars, not a backlog: expand enterprise and GCC revenue, protect reliability and retention in the core Indian base, and prove the forecasting technology was a real moat before Series C diligence began in January. Everyone nodded. What nobody had done, in the eight weeks since, was change how engineering work actually got chosen. Each product manager still scored their own items on Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort in one shared spreadsheet, sorted by RICE score whenever a decision was needed. The trouble, as Ananya had begun to see it, was that RICE compared items that were not comparable. An item that helped one enormous client scored low on Reach almost by definition, however strategic it was, while a small, easy fix touching every one of the forty-six existing customers could out-score it without being strategic at all. Robert saw this as evidence the process was broken and sales judgement should override it. In Toronto, data scientist Kwame Mensah worried that a forecasting model he believed central to the Series C pitch was being crowded out by "spreadsheet noise" — small tickets that each scored respectably but added up to nothing a board would remember. In Singapore, Farah Iqbal watched escalations rise from precisely the accounts the company could least afford to lose, and worried nobody spoke as loudly for customers who churned quietly. Ananya's task was not to find more information; the situation was, in that sense, complete. It was to decide what principle would settle it.

4. The people

Robert Fein, Head of Global Sales, based in Edison, New Jersey, had built his 2026 quota around closing two more Gulf hypermarket logos on the strength of the Wahat reference. He wanted the Arabic right-to-left invoicing and AED-currency pack, plus custom category-manager dashboards Wahat had been promised verbally, pushed to the very top of the October build, ahead of anything else.

Kwame Mensah, Lead Data Scientist, based in Toronto, had spent eighteen months on a transformer-based demand-forecasting model that, in back-testing against eleven customers' data, cut forecast error from 18 percent to roughly 11 percent. He wanted a full quarter of capacity to ship it, arguing that Belan's entire valuation premise depended on accuracy no Indian competitor could match.

Farah Iqbal, Director of Customer Success, based in Singapore, managed every account outside India, including Wahat. She wanted the pricing API's latency fixed — it had breached the 99.9 percent uptime clause in three contracts during the Ramadan sales spike — before it triggered further service-credit clawbacks or a client walking at renewal.

Elena Voss, Lead Product Designer, based in Berlin, had just finished user research showing category managers found the self-serve dashboard confusing enough that many gave up and asked their account manager to pull reports, an unpriced support cost. She wanted the insights builder redesigned, calling it a slow, compounding drag on every customer's experience.

6. The options

Option A: Keep sorting the shared backlog by raw RICE score. This is the least disruptive path — scoring already exists, and the ranking is mechanical rather than political. Its cost is exactly what Exhibit 1 shows: the two items tied to Belan's largest deal fall to the bottom, and Ananya would have to explain why a bulk SKU upload outranked the Wahat relationship.

Option B: Let Robert's request override the list this once. Pushing the localisation pack and Wahat dashboards to the top protects the largest renewal in the company's history immediately, and is easy to defend at the next board meeting. Its cost is that it resolves nothing structurally: Farah's and Kwame's work simply wait for whoever shouts loudest next quarter, and every product manager learns a scored backlog is negotiable if you escalate hard enough.

Option C: Group the backlog into the three board themes, cap capacity per theme, and rank with RICE only inside each theme. This is what Exhibits 2 and 3 show. Its upside: every stated priority gets a guaranteed, bounded share of the quarter, including the Gulf deal, without any one theme consuming the whole roadmap. Its cost is political: Kwame does not get the full quarter he wanted, Elena's redesign is deferred, and Ananya must tell four capable people their item did not lose on merit but on a ceiling set before scoring began.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why does ranking Belan's backlog by RICE score alone produce a list no one at the company, including the product managers who scored it, actually believes is right?
  2. What does each of Arjun Mehta's three strategic themes actually ask the roadmap to prove, and how would you state each as a measurable outcome rather than a slogan?
  3. If you were Ananya, how would you set the capacity ceiling for each theme in Exhibit 2 — and what would you say to Kwame, whose item loses capacity despite scoring reasonably on RICE?
  4. Which option should Ananya take into the Mumbai offsite on 20 September, and what would you tell Robert if he pushes back in the room?

8. A note for the learner

The lens this case asks you to use is simple to state and easy to skip under deadline pressure: prioritisation should follow strategy, not the volume of the request. RICE scoring is useful because it forces a proposer to be explicit about reach, impact, confidence and effort — but a single flat ranking across very different kinds of bets, as Exhibit 1 shows, breaks down whenever one item's reach is "everyone" and another's is "one enormous account." That is not a flaw to patch by overriding the score for whoever argues hardest, which is Option B in disguise; it is a sign the items being compared belong to different outcomes and need grouping before ranking.

A well-reasoned answer does three things in order. First, it takes the strategy the board agreed to — expand enterprise and GCC revenue, protect reliability and retention, prove the forecasting IP — and restates each pillar as a guiding policy with a measurable outcome this quarter, the discipline behind Rumelt's kernel: a diagnosis and a policy, not a wish. Second, it groups scored items under those outcomes, as Exhibit 2 does, so RICE does what it is good at — ranking comparable items within one theme — instead of comparing a localisation pack against a SKU upload on a single number. Third, it sets a capacity ceiling per theme before any individual score, so no theme, however loudly its sponsor advocates, can consume the whole quarter.

On that reasoning, Option C is the defensible path. It gives Robert's deal a guaranteed, bounded place — ten of thirty person-weeks, funding both the localisation pack and the dashboards — without letting sales pressure decide the rest of the quarter, and gives Farah's and Kwame's work each a themed home with its own outcome measure, rather than one contest they would have had to win outright. The uncomfortable part, worth rehearsing before the Mumbai offsite, is telling Kwame that eighteen months of research is funded but not finished this quarter, and telling Elena that sound user-research evidence did not make this quarter's ceiling. That is what it means for prioritisation to follow strategy rather than the loudest voice: someone still has to say no to people who are right about their own item and wrong only about how many other right items exist. Once the roadmap is organised this way, sequencing what is funded Now against what waits for Next is a separate decision this grouping makes far easier.

Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation

How a prioritised backlog can be arithmetically correct and strategically useless at the same time — and what to put between the strategy and the scores.

1 · The meetingThe ranked list that nobody could defend

On the morning of 14 January 2026, Devika Raghunathan sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Mehak Retail Systems' office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, looking at a spreadsheet she had asked for and now regretted. Mehak sells store-operations software — billing, stock, staff rostering, promotions — to Indian retail chains: supermarket groups in Tier-2 cities, regional pharmacy networks, apparel chains with two hundred outlets. The company had closed the previous financial year at roughly ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue across 340 customers, and Devika, its VP of Product for the past eleven months, had thirteen weeks and about 260 engineer-weeks of discretionary capacity to spend.

The spreadsheet held 214 backlog items, every one of them scored with RICE — the arithmetic that multiplies Reach (how many units are affected in a period) by Impact (how much each is affected, on a fixed scale) by Confidence (a discount for how much you actually know), then divides by Effort. Her group product managers had done the work honestly. Nobody had inflated a number. The list was sorted, and Devika could not defend the top of it.

The reason mattered. Six weeks earlier the leadership team had agreed on a diagnosis: Mehak was losing mid-market chains — those with ₹50 crore to ₹500 crore of turnover — at 18 per cent annual logo churn, against 6 per cent for its largest accounts. The post-mortems all said the same thing in different words. Mehak won the pilot in four stores and lost the rollout at forty, because store staff in Nashik or Warangal could not be trained fast enough and the chain's operations head quietly reverted to the old system. From that diagnosis came a guiding policy, in the language of Richard Rumelt's Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011): win the rollout, not the pilot; make the first ninety days after signature the strongest period in the product's life.

Not one of the top five items on the RICE list had anything to do with the first ninety days. If Devika shipped the list as ranked, she would spend a quarter and be able to say, truthfully, that every decision had been scored. She would also arrive at the April board meeting with churn unchanged and no story. The missing piece was not better scoring. It was a layer between the strategy and the scores.

2 · The ideaWhat a strategic theme is, and what it is for

A strategic theme is a named change in the world that the company has decided to buy this period, stated as an outcome with a measurable current value and a target, and given a share of delivery capacity before any individual piece of work is scored. Outcome-based prioritisation is the practice of ranking work inside those themes rather than across the whole backlog, so that the scoring arithmetic allocates within a strategic decision instead of substituting for one.

The problem it was invented to solve is specific and recurring. Scoring frameworks are relative-value machines: they compare items to each other. They have no opinion about which comparisons are worth making. A backlog that has accumulated for two years contains the residue of every previous strategy, every escalated customer complaint, and every engineer's pet cleanup, and a global ranking of that pile reproduces its history, not the company's intent. Worse, scoring is biased by construction toward work with wide, easily-counted reach and small effort — which is disproportionately the work that improves an existing motion rather than the work that changes one.

The ideas have separate parentage and were joined later. Outcome thinking in planning descends from management by objectives as practised at Intel under Andy Grove in the 1970s and carried into technology companies by John Doerr; theme-based roadmapping was popularised in product management writing through the 2010s by practitioners such as Roman Pichler and Jared Spool, largely as a reaction against roadmaps that were lists of dated features. RICE itself is newer and narrower: it was published by Sean McBride at Intercom in 2016 as an internal scoring rubric. Rumelt's kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — supplies the missing upstream piece, because a theme, properly derived, is simply one of the coherent actions the guiding policy implies.

“We are not ranking the backlog. We agreed what we are buying this quarter, we bought capacity for it, and RICE decides what goes inside each purchase.”

3 · MechanicsThe six steps, including the three people skip

The first step is to write the themes from the guiding policy, downwards. Devika's policy said win the rollout. The coherent actions that followed were: get new stores transacting sooner; make store staff able to operate without calling support; remove the security and procurement friction that stalls large chains; and keep the platform from degrading while the other three happen. Those became four themes. Note what they are not: they are not Billing, Onboarding, Security and Platform. Those are areas of the product and sections of the org chart. A theme is phrased as a change: new stores reach daily use in six weeks instead of fourteen.

The second step, the first one usually skipped, is to attach exactly one outcome metric to each theme, with a current reading and a target. Mehak's T1 metric was the median number of days from contract signature to 80 per cent of a chain's stores transacting daily: currently 96 days, target 45 by the end of Q2. T2 was support tickets per store per month: 3.4, target 1.5. T3 was the median elapsed days a deal spends in a customer's security review: 31, target 14. T4 was p95 stock-sync latency and count of Sev-1 incidents. Without a number and a target, a theme is a slogan, and a slogan cannot be failed.

The third step, also usually skipped, is to allocate capacity across themes before anybody looks at scores. Devika's team had 260 discretionary engineer-weeks. They split them 40 / 25 / 15 / 20 across T1 to T4 — 104, 65, 39 and 52 engineer-weeks. The sequence matters more than the split. If you score first and allocate afterwards, the scores anchor the conversation and the allocation becomes a description of the ranking rather than a decision about the strategy.

The fourth step is the familiar one: score candidates with RICE, but only against the other candidates in the same theme. The fifth step is the one that generates most of the method's value and is almost never written down: when nothing in a theme fits its budget, you do not raise the budget — you slice the work until something does. Budget pressure inside a theme is what converts a twelve-week ambition into a four-week first increment that still moves the metric. The sixth step is to read the outcome metrics back at the end of the period and ask whether the theme moved, which is a different and harder question than whether the work shipped.

4 · The arithmeticTwo passes over the same eight candidates

Devika's team shortlisted eight items. RICE was computed as Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort, with Impact on the conventional scale (3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low), Confidence as a decimal, Effort in engineer-weeks.

Now change one input and watch the answer move. Field data arrived in the second week of planning: the offline-first billing item, B, had been scored on a reach of 4,200 stores, but only 1,100 stores actually ran on connectivity below the threshold where the current client fails. For those 1,100, however, the problem is not medium but massive. Re-scored honestly: 1,100 × 3 × 0.7 ÷ 120 = 19.25 — lower than the 24.5 it started with, and still last in its theme. Yet those 1,100 stores accounted for 62 per cent of the mid-market logos Mehak lost last year. RICE has told the truth and produced the wrong answer, because a ratio weighted by breadth systematically under-prices concentrated severity. The theme is the corrective: if T2's outcome metric is tickets per store across the whole base, B stays out; if the metric is rollout completion in bottom-quartile-connectivity districts — which is what the guiding policy actually cares about — B becomes the theme's leading candidate and the arithmetic simply reveals that it needs slicing.

5 · NuancesEight distinctions that separate use from vocabulary

A theme is a change, not a container

The most common degradation is a theme named after a part of the product or a part of the organisation. Search, Billing and Mobile are containers: every backlog item has a natural home in one, which means the themes exclude nothing and therefore decide nothing. A real theme is a proposition about the world changing — new stores reach daily use in six weeks — and the test is whether a well-liked item can fail to belong to any theme. If nothing fails, you have a taxonomy.

Allocation before scoring, not after

The order of operations is the mechanism. Allocating capacity after seeing scores produces a split that ratifies the ranking; allocating before forces the leadership team to state, in public and in numbers, what proportion of the quarter the strategy is worth. This is uncomfortable, which is the point. Devika's 40/25/15/20 was argued over for two hours; the argument was the planning.

Themes make incommensurability visible instead of hiding it

Look again at Exhibit 1. Item E's reach is 140 deals; item H's is 6,000 stores. Dividing one by the other is meaningless, and a global sort does exactly that — which is why E lands last with a score of 4.5. Inside T3, where every candidate is measured in deals, the comparison is legitimate. The rule follows: reach units must be commensurate within a theme, and need not be across themes, because themes are never compared by score.

Themes are derived top-down; clustering the backlog is not the same operation

A tempting shortcut is to group the existing 214 items by affinity and call the clusters themes. This produces a faithful map of the backlog's history. Since the backlog's history is precisely the thing the strategy is trying to change, the clusters will look reasonable and will fund last year's priorities.

One metric per theme, with a reading and a target

Two metrics per theme means the theme can always claim success on one. A company-level metric — NPS, revenue, retention — is worse than useless as a theme metric, because it moves for a dozen reasons and cannot be attributed. The diagnostic question is: if this theme's work shipped and nothing else in the company changed, would this number move within the period?

Three to five themes, and the reason is arithmetic

At 260 engineer-weeks, seven themes give each an average of 37 engineer-weeks — less than a squad-quarter, below the size at which anything strategic can be attempted. The cap on theme count is not a stylistic preference; it is set by capacity divided by the smallest useful unit of work.

The unthemed residue is information

Items D and F did not belong to any theme. That is a finding with two legitimate readings. Either the strategy has a genuine gap — and the right response is to amend the themes, not to smuggle the work in — or the request is real but not this quarter's business, and should be declined in those words. What destroys the method is the third response: creating a fifth theme called Customer Requests so nothing has to be refused.

What themes cannot tell you

Themes will not sequence work within the quarter, will not resolve technical dependencies, and will not tell you whether the strategy is correct. They are a faithful transmission mechanism, which means a wrong strategy executed through good themes fails faster and more thoroughly than a wrong strategy executed through a scattered backlog. That is usually an advantage, but it should be understood before it is admired.

6 · ContextConsumer, B2B and marketplace; small company and large

In B2B software like Mehak's, themes are relatively easy to name and hard to fund, because named accounts apply continuous pressure and every escalation arrives with revenue attached. The theme's function is mostly defensive: it gives a product leader a principled way to say no to a ₹3 crore account without saying “your request scored badly”. In consumer products — the situation at Mithila Play, a Pune streaming company — reach is large and uniform, so RICE scores cluster and discriminate poorly; themes do more work there, because they are often the only thing distinguishing two items whose scores differ by five per cent and whose strategic meaning differs entirely.

Marketplaces are the genuinely different case. At Mitraa Bazaar, an artisan-goods marketplace operating out of Jaipur, any theme stated for one side has an effect on the other, and a theme like reduce buyer time-to-first-purchase can be delivered by work that raises seller cost. Marketplace themes therefore need to be stated as a pair with a constraint — an outcome for one side and a guardrail metric for the other — or the arithmetic will quietly optimise liquidity out of the system.

Stage changes the emphasis rather than the method. A thirty-person company usually has one theme, often unstated, and the discipline it needs is to say the theme out loud and notice how much work does not serve it. A company of Mehak's size needs the capacity split because it has enough teams that unallocated capacity drifts toward whoever escalates hardest. A very large company faces the opposite problem: themes proliferate to satisfy every executive, budgets become symbolic, and the meaningful decision migrates back to headcount planning.

7 · MistakesFour failures and the cheapest test for each

Themes applied as labels after the fact. The symptom is a backlog where every item carries a theme tag and the distribution closely matches last quarter's delivery. The misunderstanding is treating themes as classification rather than allocation. The diagnostic costs one question in a planning review: name something we declined this quarter because of the theme it belonged to. Silence is the finding.

A capacity split that is never enforced. The symptom is a planning deck that says 40/25/15/20 and a delivery record that does not. The misunderstanding is that stating a budget is the same as spending one. The diagnostic is to reconstruct last quarter's actual split from merged work and compare; at Mehak this took an analyst half a day and showed 11 per cent against a theme budgeted at 25.

Outcome metrics that nobody owns or that move on their own. The symptom is a quarterly review where the theme metric improved and nobody can say why, or degraded and everybody blames seasonality. The misunderstanding is confusing a company outcome with a theme outcome. The diagnostic is the attribution question posed above.

Scoring across themes on one list. The symptom is a single global RICE-sorted sheet with a theme column added. The misunderstanding is that a theme is a property of an item rather than a budget it competes within. The diagnostic: check whether the lowest-scoring funded item in the most important theme beat the highest-scoring unfunded item in the least important one. If it did not, the themes are decorative.

8 · What good looks like

Handled well, the January meeting is short and the argument happens earlier. Four themes are on one page with a current reading, a target and a percentage of capacity, agreed by the leadership team before any PM opens a scoring sheet. Each theme has a named owner who will report the metric in April whether or not it moved. Scoring sheets exist per theme, not per company. Three items in the shortlist are visibly smaller than their original proposals, and the product managers can explain what was cut and what evidence would justify buying the rest. Two well-supported requests have been declined in writing, with the theme they failed to serve named. Roughly a quarter of capacity is deliberately unspent at planning time. And when a large chain escalates in February, the conversation is about whether the escalation changes the diagnosis — not about whether the escalation outranks the roadmap.

9 · DecisionWhat Devika did, and what to read next

Devika took the theme-budgeted plan to the leadership meeting on 21 January and made two additional moves. She changed T2's outcome metric from support tickets per store to rollout completion in bottom-quartile-connectivity districts, which reordered the theme and put the offline-billing work at the top of it, sliced to a 44-week first increment covering the six states where those 1,100 stores were concentrated. And she declined the loyalty-programme builder in writing to both requesting accounts, offering the theme reasoning rather than the score, and recorded the request as evidence for a possible fifth theme in the following half-year if the pattern recurred. Her reasoning was simple: the arithmetic had been correct and the allocation had been absent, and only one of those two problems was worth a quarter of engineering to fix.

What to learn next follows the same chain. RICE scoring repays a closer look, because most of the disputes inside a theme turn out to be disputes about how reach was counted. Rumelt's kernel is upstream: if the guiding policy is vague, the themes will be containers no matter how carefully they are written. And roadmaps in Now / Next / Later form are what themes unlock — a roadmap organised by theme and horizon rather than by date makes a commitment about outcomes that a Gantt chart of features cannot.

Two questions to sit with. First: in your own last planning cycle, what was declined, and can you name the strategic reason rather than the score? Second: if your themes were correct but your strategy was wrong, how long would it take you to find out — and would the theme metrics you have chosen be the thing that told you?

Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation

A theme budget is a price. Until a product leader can say what price they are paying, and say it in the same units the scoring sheet uses, they have made an assertion rather than a decision.

1 · Two roomsMumbai, 9 February; Gurugram, 12 February

Arundhati Sen had run the Q4 planning meeting at Mehul Payments four times before and had never had to argue about the split. Mehul, founded in 2016 and now headquartered in Lower Parel, sells payment orchestration, reconciliation and dispute-management software to Indian banks and large merchants; it had closed FY25 at about ₹310 crore of revenue, and its engineering organisation of roughly 190 people had, after on-call, incident load and compliance overhead were taken out, about 700 engineer-weeks of discretionary capacity for the quarter beginning in April. As Chief Product Officer, Arundhati had spent eighteen months moving the company's identity from orchestration — a crowded business where the differentiator is a connector list — towards reconciliation, where switching costs are real. The strategy was written down and the leadership team believed it.

The problem in the room on 9 February was that her own scoring sheet argued against her. Reconciliation had seven strong candidates for the quarter, several of them cheap, and the dispute-management work — the second half of the same strategic bet, and the half that fourteen bank customers representing roughly ₹18 crore of at-risk annual recurring revenue kept complaining about — produced scores that looked mediocre next to them. So did the statutory work that Mehul had no choice about. If she fenced capacity for disputes, she would be overruling the arithmetic, and her VP of Engineering had asked the obvious question: by how much? Arundhati did not have a number, and she recognised that not having one was the actual gap.

Three days later and sixteen hundred kilometres north, Kabir Deshmukh faced a structurally different version of the same problem at Mitali Fresh, a Gurugram company that runs a fresh-produce marketplace connecting farmer-producer organisations and neighbourhood retailers to about 3.1 million monthly transacting buyers across nine cities, on annualised gross merchandise value of roughly ₹1,420 crore. Mitali Fresh had nine squads and about 380 engineer-weeks a quarter. Kabir's highest-scoring candidate by a wide margin was a reorder nudge carrying a ₹40 discount; it would almost certainly move the buyer-habit metric his company had made its headline outcome for the year, and it would almost as certainly push contribution margin per order, already at minus ₹34, further into the red. Two of his four themes wanted opposite things, and the scoring sheet was silent on the conflict because a score has no opinion about side effects.

2 · The ideaDefinition, lineage, and the four camps

A strategic theme is a named change in the world that an organisation has decided to buy in a given period, expressed as an outcome with a current reading and a target, and granted a share of delivery capacity before any individual item of work is scored. Outcome-based prioritisation is the discipline of ranking candidates inside those envelopes rather than across the whole backlog, so that the scoring arithmetic performs allocation within a strategic choice instead of substituting for the choice itself.

The problem the construct addresses is structural, not cultural. Scoring frameworks are relative-value machines: they compare candidates to one another and are indifferent to which comparisons are worth making. A mature backlog is a sediment of every previous strategy, every escalation that arrived with revenue attached, and every engineer's accumulated irritation with the codebase; a global ranking of that sediment faithfully reproduces its history. Worse, any score of the form value-divided-by-effort is biased by construction toward broad, cheaply-counted reach and small effort, which is systematically the work that improves an existing motion rather than the work that changes one. New strategies almost always require expensive work with narrow initial reach. They therefore lose global rankings by design.

The lineage is composite. Outcome-denominated planning descends from management by objectives as practised at Intel under Andy Grove in the 1970s and carried into technology companies by John Doerr. Theme-based roadmapping was popularised through the 2010s by practitioners including Roman Pichler and Jared Spool as a reaction against roadmaps that were dated feature lists. RICE — Reach times Impact times Confidence divided by Effort — was published by Sean McBride at Intercom in 2016 as an internal rubric and spread rapidly because it is easy to compute. Richard Rumelt's kernel from Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011) — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — supplies the missing upstream element: a properly derived theme is one of the coherent actions that a guiding policy implies, and nothing else.

Competent practitioners disagree about this, sharply, and the disagreement is worth stating precisely because it recurs in every planning argument.

The allocation school holds that the central act of prioritisation is allocating capacity to strategic bets, and that ranking items is a subordinate, almost clerical activity. It will sign: a strategy that has not been expressed as a percentage of delivery capacity has not been funded. It will not sign: an item's score should be able to move capacity between themes.

The single-ranking school holds that a ranking is the only artefact that can actually be executed, and that fenced budgets defer the real decision to whoever runs the sprint. It will sign: if two things cannot be compared, one of them is not ready to be worked on. It will not sign: capacity should be fenced for a theme regardless of the quality of the candidates available in it. Its strongest evidence is empirical: fenced budgets reliably get spent, including on weak work, because a budget with a deadline is a use-it-or-lose-it instrument.

The outcome-contract school, which is where most OKR practice sits, holds that teams should be given outcome targets and autonomy, not capacity envelopes. It will sign: tell a team what number to move and let them decide what to build. It will not sign: a central planner should decide the percentage split between themes. Its complaint against the allocation school is that a capacity fence is a solution-space commitment disguised as a strategy commitment.

The continuous-discovery school, associated with Marty Cagan's product-bet framing and Teresa Torres's opportunity-solution trees, is more radical: quarterly capacity splits presume you know enough about the solution space to price it, and you usually do not. It will sign: fund an opportunity and a team, and let the tree be pruned weekly. It will not sign: score before you discover.

The flow-economics school, descending from Don Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) and embodied in SAFe's weighted-shortest-job-first, holds that work should be sequenced strictly by cost of delay divided by duration, and that theme fences destroy economic sequencing. It will sign: economics, not politics, sequences work. It will not sign: fence a quarter of capacity for a theme whose best candidate has poor economics.

These are not reconcilable by synthesis, and a page that pretends otherwise is not helping. What follows takes the allocation school's construct seriously and then asks the flow school's question of it — what is the fence costing? — because that question turns out to have a computable answer, and computing it is the single move that most separates expert practice from vocabulary.

3 · Mechanics in depthThe theme budget is a constraint, and constraints have prices

Begin with an arithmetic correction that most teams never make. RICE is a rate: expected value per unit of effort. Reach times Impact times Confidence is the numerator — call it the item's nominal value, V — and Effort E is the denominator, so RICE equals V / E. It follows that adding up RICE scores across a portfolio is meaningless, and that the quantity a quarter actually buys is the sum of V, not the sum of scores. Once this is seen, the planning problem has an obvious formal shape: choose a subset of candidates maximising total V subject to a capacity constraint. It is a knapsack, and if the items are small relative to capacity the greedy solution — rank by V/E, fill from the top — is close to optimal.

The interesting quantity is what happens at the boundary. In the relaxed version of that problem, the item at the margin defines a threshold rate, conventionally written λ*: the value per engineer-week of the least valuable work the quarter can still afford. Anything above λ* is funded; anything below is not. λ* is the shadow price of engineering capacity, and it is the number a product organisation is implicitly quoting every time it says no.

Adding theme budgets replaces one capacity constraint with several. Each theme k now has its own marginal item and therefore its own shadow price λk. If the fences did nothing, every λk would equal λ*. They never do, and the divergence is precisely the strategic assertion being made. A theme whose λk is below λ* is being over-funded relative to nominal value — the organisation is buying work worth less per week than work it is declining elsewhere. The ratio λ* / λk is the implied strategic multiplier: the factor by which leadership is asserting that a unit of nominal value in theme k is worth more than a unit anywhere else.

When nothing in a theme fits its envelope, the disciplined response is not to widen the envelope but to cut the candidate until it fits — and because RICE has effort in the denominator, a well-chosen slice usually scores higher than the original. Teams that plan with slack never discover this, which is one reason experienced planners set theme budgets deliberately a little tight. The second is that the implied multiplier is a public number and therefore a governance instrument: once leadership has seen that the disputes fence prices a value unit at seven times the company average, they can either affirm it — which is a real strategic commitment, recorded — or revise the split, which is also fine. What they can no longer do is agree to a strategy and quietly not fund it.

4 · When it appliesFour testable conditions, applied to both companies

The construct is not universally appropriate, and its preconditions can be written as claims that are true or false of a given organisation rather than as advice.

Claim one: there exists a written guiding policy from which three to five coherent actions can be derived without invention. True at Mehul: the move from orchestration to reconciliation generates recon, disputes and reliability as obvious consequences. Partially true at Mitali Fresh, where the stated policy — become the default weekly grocery for households in nine cities — generates a buyer theme and a supply theme cleanly but says nothing about unit economics, which arrived as a theme from the board rather than from the policy. That gap is not fatal but it is worth naming, because a theme without a parent in the guiding policy tends to lose arguments it should win.

Claim two: delivery capacity is large enough that capacity divided by the number of themes exceeds the minimum size of a meaningful bet. At Mehul, 700 weeks across four themes averages 175 — comfortably more than a squad-quarter. At Mitali Fresh, 380 across four averages 95, which is close to the floor; the platform theme at 38 weeks is arguably too small to be a bet at all and functions as a maintenance reserve. An organisation of thirty engineers that declares five themes has declared five aspirations.

Claim three: outcomes are attributable to work within the period. This is where the construct is weakest and least often tested. Mehul's dispute-cycle metric responds within weeks and is attributable. Mitali Fresh's third-order-within-thirty-days metric has a thirty-day measurement lag on top of a build cycle, which means a theme funded in April produces its first honest reading in July. Where the lag exceeds the planning period, theme metrics must be supplemented by leading indicators chosen in advance, or the review degenerates into narrative.

Claim four: the organisation can actually decline work. A capacity fence is only real if something is refused. In companies where any sufficiently senior escalation is honoured, themes become a routing table: work is reclassified into whichever theme still has budget, and the system produces the appearance of discipline with none of the substance.

There are also situations where themes are actively misleading. In a genuine crisis — a security breach, a payment outage, a regulator's show-cause notice — the correct structure is a single objective and an unfenced organisation, and imposing a theme split wastes the coordination advantage a crisis temporarily provides. In a company searching for product-market fit, themes formalise a hypothesis about where value lies, which is exactly the thing still unknown; the continuous-discovery school's objection is strongest here and should simply be conceded. And in a pure platform or infrastructure team whose customers are other internal teams, an outcome metric is often a fiction because the outcome belongs to someone else's product.
