The multi-product seam appears at Mehul, which runs three business units with separate P&Ls. T2, disputes, spans two of them. A theme that crosses a unit boundary is funded by whichever unit hosts the work, which means the hosting unit pays for a corporate bet out of its own local capacity and its own local themes starve. Companies describe the solution as “alignment”; what mature ones actually do is carve cross-cutting themes off the top, before unit budgets are set, with a named accountable executive who is not a unit head. Mehul had not done this, and T2's awkward position in the scoring sheet was partly an artefact of that omission rather than a genuine statement about value.

The regulated case is cleaner than it looks. Mehnaaz Insure Cloud, a Chennai company selling policy-administration software to general insurers, faces a steady stream of mandatory changes originating with the regulator and with industry bodies. These are not themes: a theme names an outcome the company has chosen, and a mandate offers no choice and no target beyond compliance by a date. Mehnaaz's practice — and Arundhati adopted the same discipline for Mehul's T3 — is to compute the mandate load as a tax taken off the top and to state the number: in Mehnaaz's case, 22 per cent of engineering capacity for the year. Stating it converts an invisible drain into a budget line that can be attacked with automation, which is how the 22 per cent became 15 per cent over two years.

The hardware-plus-software seam forces a change to the period itself. Mehrab Instruments, a Pune manufacturer of point-of-care diagnostic devices with companion clinic software, set a theme worth setting: a clinic obtains its first valid result in under twenty minutes, against a current median of 47 minutes. Decomposition showed that software could remove about 16 minutes — sample-entry redesign, pre-warming, result auto-transmission — and the remaining 11 minutes required a cartridge change with an 18-month tooling and validation cycle. A quarterly capacity fence cannot express that. Mehrab's answer was to give themes a horizon attribute: programme themes carry a standing allocation across six quarters and are reviewed half-yearly, while quarterly themes hold the software-only increments. The metric is decomposed accordingly, so the quarterly theme owns 47 → 31 minutes and the programme theme owns 31 → 19.

The AI-native case breaks the denominator. At Mitrika AI, a Bengaluru company selling an autonomous support agent to consumer-internet firms, fourteen eval-driven improvement items in a single quarter had a planned median effort of six engineer-weeks and an actual interquartile range of three to nineteen, because whether a quality target is reachable is discovered during the work rather than before it. Effort-denominated budgets overran in 38 per cent of themes. Mitrika's adaptation was to budget in whole squad-quarters rather than engineer-weeks — three squads on the quality theme, one on integrations — and to attach a week-five checkpoint at which a theme either shows movement on its eval metric or surrenders a squad. The second half of that rule is what makes the first half honest.

6 · NuancesNine distinctions, each with its tell

The fence is a price, and the expert can quote it

The observable difference between someone who has internalised this and someone who has read about it is a single sentence: this split prices a dispute-management value unit at seven times a reconciliation one, and I believe that because of the fourteen accounts. The competent practitioner defends the split with a story. The expert defends it with the story and the multiplier, and knows which of the two would change their mind.

RICE is a rate; the portfolio buys the numerator

Summing or averaging RICE scores is a category error that appears in a remarkable number of planning decks. The tell is a slide reporting “average RICE of committed work: 64”, which is a number with no interpretation. Experts ask what total nominal value the quarter buys and how it is distributed, and they notice that a quarter full of small high-rate items can buy less total value than a quarter with two large ones.

Slicing under budget pressure is the value-creating step

Teams treat “it doesn't fit the theme budget” as an obstacle. It is the method working. Because effort sits in the denominator, cutting a twelve-week ambition to a four-week increment that moves the metric usually raises the score, and it converts a bet into an experiment. The tell is a planning round in which at least a third of funded items are visibly smaller than their original proposals and the product managers can name what was cut and what evidence would buy the rest.

Confidence is doing two incompatible jobs

In RICE, the confidence factor absorbs both estimation uncertainty (we have not measured the reach) and strategic uncertainty (the market may move). These behave differently: the first is reducible by a week of research, the second is not reducible at all. Experts split them, keeping a research discount inside the score and handling strategic uncertainty at the theme level as a hypothesis to be reviewed. A single 0.5 that means both things hides the only question worth asking, which is whether anyone can cheaply make it a 0.9.

Reach units must be commensurate inside a theme and need not be across

At Mehul, c1's reach is measured in bank integrations and d1's in transactions per quarter. Dividing one by the other is nonsense, and a global ranking does exactly that. Inside a theme, where candidates share a beneficiary and a metric, the comparison is legitimate. This is a substantial and under-appreciated argument for themes that has nothing to do with strategy: they restore the conditions under which the arithmetic means anything.

A theme names a change, not a container

The degenerate form is a theme named after a product area or an org unit — Search, Billing, Mobile — under which every backlog item finds a natural home. Themes that exclude nothing decide nothing. The diagnostic is whether a well-liked item can fail to belong to any theme; if none can, the scheme is a taxonomy wearing a strategy's clothes.

Unthemed work is a finding with exactly two honest readings

Either the strategy has a genuine gap, in which case the themes should be amended in public, or the request is legitimate but not this period's business, in which case it should be declined in writing with the theme it failed to serve named. The dishonest third option — a fifth theme called Customer Requests — converts the system into a filing cabinet. Experts keep a declined log and read it at the next re-derivation; the pattern in the log is often the best available evidence that a theme is missing.

Themes transmit strategy faithfully, including a wrong one

This is the property that makes the construct dangerous as well as useful. A well-run theme system executes a mistaken guiding policy more completely and more quickly than a scattered backlog would have. The corrective is a falsification clause: every theme carries a written hypothesis of the form we believe moving X will move Y because Z, and a rule that a theme whose metric reaches target while Y does not move triggers a review of the diagnosis rather than a celebration.

Enforce at the right granularity

A capacity fence is a quarterly instrument. Enforcing it at sprint level — blocking a ticket because its theme is over budget this fortnight — destroys flow and teaches teams to mislabel work. The tell of good practice is that nobody polices the split during the quarter and somebody reconstructs it from delivered work afterwards, comparing intent to actuals. At Mehul this reconstruction took an analyst half a day and showed that the previous year's disputes theme, budgeted at 20 per cent, had actually received 11.

7 · Across product types and stages

In enterprise and B2B software the naming of themes is easy and the funding of them is hard, because every escalation arrives with a contract value attached and a global ranking will always find a ₹3 crore account more compelling than an unbuilt capability. The theme's primary function is defensive: it supplies a principled refusal that does not require telling a customer their request scored badly. In consumer products the opposite holds — reach is large and uniform, scores cluster tightly, and two items separated by five per cent of score may differ completely in strategic meaning; here themes are often the only thing doing real discrimination. Platforms and marketplaces need the paired-guardrail structure of Exhibit 2 or they will optimise one side into a liquidity failure. Hardware needs the horizon attribute of the Mehrab example. AI products need the squad-quarter denominator and the mid-period checkpoint.

Stage changes emphasis more than substance, and it is worth saying plainly where it does not change anything: the requirement that a theme be phrased as a change rather than a container, and that it carry one attributable metric, is identical at thirty engineers and three thousand. What changes is the binding constraint. A small company usually has one real theme and its discipline problem is admitting that, then noticing how much work does not serve it. A company of Mehul's size needs the fences because unallocated capacity drifts toward whoever escalates hardest. A very large company faces the opposite pathology: themes multiply to satisfy every executive, each fence becomes too small to matter, and the meaningful allocation quietly migrates back into annual headcount planning, where it is invisible to the product organisation entirely.

8 · Three worked cases, including one that failed

The first is Mehul's, already computed. The fences cost roughly 2,200 nominal value units of discretionary allocation and bought a funded attempt at a ₹18 crore retention problem. Whether that is a good trade depends on a translation between value units and rupees that Mehul cannot perform, and being explicit about the untranslatability was more useful to the leadership team than a fabricated conversion would have been.

The second is Mitali Fresh's guardrail arithmetic, also above: a candidate scoring 3.7 times its nearest rival was funded at roughly a third of its intended incentive and with its confidence factor halved, because the theme system made a cross-theme side effect visible that a single ranked list would have hidden entirely.

The third is a failure, and it is the more instructive case because the mechanics were followed correctly throughout. Mitrata Learning, a Hyderabad company selling exam-preparation software to students and to coaching institutes, adopted themes in 2023 and enforced them rigorously. Its dominant theme, allocated 45 per cent of capacity, was students complete the courses they start, with course completion rate as the metric. Over three quarters the team moved completion from 41 per cent to 63 per cent. Every review was green. Monthly churn over the same period moved from 7.8 per cent to 7.9 to 7.7 to 7.8, and institutional renewals fell.

The diagnosis, when it was finally re-run in the fourth quarter, was that the churn driver had shifted. Students were not leaving because they failed to finish courses; institutional buyers were leaving because Mitrata's reporting could not demonstrate outcomes to the institutions' own boards, and a competitor's could. The theme had been correct when written and had been carried forward unexamined through four planning cycles. The recovery was not glamorous: the leadership team re-derived themes from a fresh diagnosis, moved the split from 45/25/20/10 to 20/40/25/15, added a written hypothesis line to every theme, and instituted a rule that a theme reaching its target without the linked business metric moving triggers a diagnosis review rather than a promotion. Monthly churn reached 6.1 per cent three quarters later. The cost of catching it late was roughly a year of correctly-executed engineering aimed at a problem the company no longer had.

9 · Failure modes and their early warnings

Six failure modes recur often enough to be worth naming with their diagnostics. Themes as containers announces itself when every backlog item classifies cleanly and the resulting distribution resembles last quarter's delivery; the diagnostic is to ask a planning group to name something declined because of its theme, and silence is the finding. Caught late, it costs a year of legitimising an unchanged backlog with strategic vocabulary. Budgets stated but not enforced shows up as a planning deck with percentages that nobody ever reconciles against actuals; the diagnostic is the half-day reconstruction, and the late cost is a board that believes a strategy is funded when it is not.

Unattributable theme metrics appear whenever a theme's metric is a company-level number such as NPS or revenue; the diagnostic question is whether the number would move within the period if this theme's work shipped and nothing else in the company changed. Caught late, two quarters are spent arguing about seasonality. Frozen themes — the Mitrata failure — are visible in the planning archive as theme names unchanged across four consecutive decks; the diagnostic is to re-run the diagnosis cold, without reference to the existing themes, and see whether the same set emerges.

Mandatory work hidden inside a theme presents as a theme whose budget grows every quarter and whose metric never moves; the diagnostic is to separate items by whether the company could choose not to do them, and the late cost is a strategy that has been silently defunded by compliance. Finally, fence-induced reclassification appears as a spike in theme reassignments during the last week of planning; the diagnostic is simply to count how many items changed theme after the budgets were published. When that number is large, themes have become a routing table and the system is generating the appearance of discipline with none of its substance.

10 · Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disagreements remain live, and none of them is a misunderstanding.

The first is fences versus economics. The flow school's position, in its strongest form, is that the shadow-price computation above is an indictment rather than a defence: if the fence costs 2,200 value units, that is simply a measure of waste, and the correct response is to improve the candidate pool in the under-served theme rather than to buy weak work in it. Its evidence is the well-documented tendency of fenced budgets to be fully spent regardless of candidate quality. What would have to be true for it to be wrong is that nominal value systematically under-measures strategic value — which is exactly what one would expect when a strategy's early work has narrow reach by construction. The honest position is that both are true and the fence is a bet on the second effect exceeding the first.

The second is capacity envelopes versus outcome contracts. The outcome-contract school argues that telling a team both what outcome to move and how many weeks it may spend is double instruction, and that the weeks constraint smuggles in solution assumptions. Its evidence is that the best-performing teams in most organisations are the ones given a number and left alone. The allocation school responds that outcome contracts without capacity envelopes are unfalsifiable at the portfolio level, because nothing prevents three teams from pursuing overlapping outcomes while a fourth strategic area goes unstaffed. For the outcome-contract position to be wrong, teams would have to be poor at self-sizing their own ambition; for the allocation position to be wrong, central planners would have to be worse.

The third is theme stability. One camp holds that themes should persist for at least a year, on the grounds that a bet abandoned after a quarter was never a bet. The other holds that quarterly re-derivation is the only protection against the Mitrata failure. Both cite real evidence: strategy churn is a documented destroyer of compounding work, and frozen themes are a documented destroyer of relevance. The field has not settled where the line sits, and the practical compromise most mature organisations reach — annual themes with half-yearly re-derivation and a written falsification clause — is a compromise rather than a resolution, and should be presented as one.

11 · What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives at planning with a theme slide. Someone who has internalised it arrives with four numbers and a written hypothesis per theme, can state the implied multiplier each fence represents, knows which of the shadow prices they would defend to a sceptical CFO and which they would concede, and has a declined log from the previous period that they read before writing the new themes. In the quarter itself they do not police the split; afterwards they reconstruct it. They set budgets slightly tight on purpose, because they know that budget pressure is what produces the slicing that produces the learning. They treat unthemed work as evidence rather than as noise. And when a theme hits its target while the business metric does not move, their first instinct is to question the diagnosis rather than to claim the win — which is, in the end, the only habit that separates a planning system from a reporting system.

12 · Decisions

Arundhati Sen made three moves. She removed the mandate work from the theme system entirely, restating it as a 25 per cent tax taken before the split and setting a two-year target to halve it through automation, which freed the remaining themes to be argued about on their merits. She published the implied multiplier for the disputes fence — roughly seven times — and asked the leadership team to affirm or revise it in writing; they affirmed it, and reduced the fence from 140 engineer-weeks to 110 after agreeing that the third candidate in the theme, the chargeback webhooks at a rate of 12, was genuinely not worth buying. And she required a hypothesis line on each theme, of which the disputes one read: we believe halving dispute cycle time will reduce mid-market bank attrition because attrition interviews name it in eleven of fourteen cases. That sentence is testable, and testing it was scheduled for October.

Kabir Deshmukh kept his four themes and his guardrails, capped the reorder incentive at ₹15 with a ninety-day holdout, and made one structural change: he moved the platform theme's 38 engineer-weeks out of the theme system and into a standing reserve, on the grounds that 38 weeks was below the size at which a bet is a bet, and that calling maintenance a strategic theme had been quietly inflating his sense of how much strategy he was actually funding. The freed allocation went to supply reliability, where the fill-rate metric had the shortest measurement lag and therefore the best chance of teaching him something before July.

Three questions for discussion.

1. Mehul's fences price a dispute-management value unit at roughly seven times a reconciliation one. Is the right response to affirm the multiplier, to shrink the fence, or to reject the entire calculation on the grounds that nominal value units are ordinal quantities that should never have been multiplied and summed in the first place?

2. Mitrata's theme was correctly derived, correctly funded and correctly delivered, and produced a year of wasted engineering. What specific artefact, produced at the time the theme was written, would have caught it in the second quarter rather than the fourth — and what would it have cost to produce?

3. Kabir's guardrails prevented a cross-theme side effect that a single ranked list would have hidden. Under what circumstances does a guardrail become a veto that prevents the company from ever making an aggressive bet, and how would you tell the two situations apart from inside the planning meeting?

13 · Going deeper

RICE scoring is the immediate next stop, because most disputes inside a theme turn out to be disputes about how reach was counted and how confidence was justified; understanding its construction is what lets you read a shadow price without being misled by it. Rumelt's kernel sits directly upstream: where the guiding policy is vague, themes become containers no matter how carefully they are worded, and no amount of downstream rigour repairs that. Roadmaps in Now / Next / Later form are what themes unlock, because a roadmap organised by theme and horizon makes a commitment about outcomes that a dated feature list cannot.

Value versus effort is the simplest form of the same arithmetic and is worth studying precisely to see what it loses relative to RICE. The Kano model supplies the missing theory of impact — why some improvements delight and others merely avoid dissatisfaction — which is what the impact factor is crudely approximating. Weighted scoring and WSJF formalise the flow school's alternative and let you steelman the position that theme fences destroy economic sequencing. Buy-a-feature is the cheapest practical way to elicit the relative weights that a theme split asserts, from customers or from executives, without an argument. User story mapping is the technique that makes slicing under budget pressure tractable rather than arbitrary. And prioritising under constraints generalises the whole construct to situations where the binding limit is not engineering weeks at all but regulatory windows, cash, or a single scarce specialist.
